“You’ll be wanting to go, then,” her mother said, without turning from the stove. Alexandra didn’t answer. The kitchen smelled of coffee and woodsmoke, and through the window she could see the fields stretching away, brown and bare under the autumn sky. “I’ve thought about it,” she said finally. “I don’t know that I’d be any good out there.” Her mother laughed shortly, wiping her hands on her apron. “You’ve never been afraid of work,” she said. “Whatever else you are.” It was not quite a blessing, but it was close enough. Alexandra crossed the room and stood beside her, and for a while they watched the kettle together, saying nothing at all.
